title: Beyond the Visual: The Impacts of Urban Soundscapes on Landscape Design and User Experience

findings.mechanism: The park's design and programming foster positive experiences.
findings.quote: 90% were satisfied or very satisfied with their experience

findings.mechanism: Seating provides comfort and opportunities for interaction/rest.
findings.quote: the top 3 general elements of impact are “seating,”

findings.mechanism: Open lawns provide space for activities and relaxation.
findings.quote: “open/event lawn,”

findings.mechanism: Water features are aesthetically pleasing and provide auditory masking.
findings.quote: “water/water features.”

findings.antecedent: Sound environment at Klyde Warren Park
findings.consequent: Perception as pleasant, vibrant, and eventful
findings.mechanism: Overall positive experience contributes to pleasant perception.
findings.quote: “pleasant,” “vibrant,” and “eventful,”

findings.antecedent: Traffic noise (e.g., cars, buses, trains, airplanes)
findings.mechanism: Traffic noise is a dominant and often unwanted sound source in urban environments.
findings.quote: “traffic noise,”... ranked as the top 3 loudest sound sources.

findings.antecedent: Sounds of individuals (e.g., conversations, laughter, children at play)
findings.mechanism: Human interaction sounds are prominent in active urban parks.
findings.quote: “sounds of individuals,”... ranked as the top 3 loudest sound sources.

findings.antecedent: Crowds of people (e.g., passers, restaurants, sports event, festivals)
findings.mechanism: Crowd sounds are expected and prominent in active urban parks.
findings.quote: “crowds of people” are ranked as the top 3 loudest sound sources.

findings.antecedent: Natural sounds (e.g., singing birds, flowing water, wind in vegetation)
findings.mechanism: Natural sounds may be masked by louder urban sounds or less prominent.
findings.quote: “natural sounds”... are perceived aurally to a lesser extent.

findings.antecedent: Material sounds (e.g., metal or wood clanking, footsteps on pavement or gravel)
findings.mechanism: Material sounds are less prominent than other urban sounds.
findings.quote: “material sounds”... are perceived aurally to a lesser extent.

findings.antecedent: Actual sound environment at Klyde Warren Park
findings.mechanism: Users associate the park's sound level with a 'noisy restaurant' environment (85 dB).
findings.quote: 85 decibels of “noisy restaurant” was the most common sound level description.

findings.consequent: Perceived appropriateness for Klyde Warren Park
findings.mechanism: The park's design and atmosphere are perceived as suitable for social interaction.
findings.quote: the top activity viewed as most appropriate for the park is tied between “socializing, conversing, chatting”

findings.antecedent: Kids play (e.g., sports, playground, splash pad) activities
findings.consequent: Perceived appropriateness for Klyde Warren Park
findings.mechanism: The park's design and atmosphere are perceived as suitable for children's play.
findings.quote: and “kids play.”

findings.consequent: Perceived appropriateness for Klyde Warren Park
findings.mechanism: The park's environment may not be ideal or preferred for these activities compared to others.
findings.quote: “Walking, jogging, running” is ranked the lowest as a good location for that activity.

findings.antecedent: Location 9 (near North Pearl Street and freeway)
findings.mechanism: Proximity to freeway and busy street increases noise.
findings.quote: location 9... emitted the highest average noise level at 77.8 dB.

findings.mechanism: Location may be more shielded or have fewer direct noise sources.
findings.quote: location 7 registered the lowest sound level at 70.2 dB.

findings.antecedent: Vicinity of a one-way street and presence of food trucks (locations 3-5)
findings.mechanism: Food trucks act as physical barriers, and one-way streets generate less noise.
findings.quote: The test areas numbered from 3-5 have recorded the second-lowest decibel average.

findings.antecedent: Location 1 (park entrance at roadway intersection) with lack of visual barriers
findings.consequent: Perceived sound level compared to actual sound level
findings.mechanism: Lack of visual barriers (cars, buildings) leads to psychological noise amplification.
findings.quote: users perceived the sound as nearly 10 decibels louder than the recorded measurement.

findings.consequent: Perceived sound level compared to actual sound level
findings.mechanism: Visual stimuli or context may influence perceived loudness.
findings.quote: locations 3, 4, and 8 were all perceived to be louder than the actual reading

findings.consequent: Perceived sound level compared to actual sound level
findings.mechanism: Perception aligns with actual measurement, possibly due to expected sounds (children playing).
findings.quote: location 2 was perceived to be a similar decibel level as the recorded measurement, at 76.8 dB.

findings.antecedent: Location 4 (main pathway between event lawn and performance stage) with programming elements
findings.mechanism: Programming elements (seating, splash pad, live piano, open lawn activities, people-watching) contribute to high satisfaction.
findings.quote: locations 4 and 8 garnered the highest satisfaction rates compared to the rest, tied at 94%.

findings.mechanism: Presence of water features and other positive visual/aural elements contribute to high satisfaction.
findings.quote: locations 4 and 8 garnered the highest satisfaction rates compared to the rest, tied at 94%.

findings.antecedent: Visual masking (vegetation, building placement, water elements)
findings.mechanism: Visual elements distract from noise, creating a psychological improvement and sense of safety.
findings.quote: Visually masking and greening urban environments can enhance the impact of unwanted sounds

findings.mechanism: Vegetation has a calming effect and acts as a visual distractor.
findings.quote: greening up [the] urban environment” can psychologically mitigate road noise.

findings.mechanism: Trees provide a calming visual effect, even without significant acoustic attenuation.
findings.quote: Trees have a great calming effect... but it is definitely a psychological improvement.”

findings.mechanism: Water provides both visual appeal and auditory masking/pleasant sounds.
findings.quote: water elements will visually and audibly enhance the user experience.

findings.consequent: Sense of safety and appreciation of park surroundings
findings.mechanism: Physical distance and visual barriers reduce perceived threat from traffic.
findings.quote: create as much of a buffer from the street as you can to get people further away.”

findings.antecedent: Strategic building orientation and land use
findings.mechanism: Buildings can act as screens or direct sound, influencing the acoustic environment.
findings.quote: Orienting buildings in specific directions... can better enhance the presence of wanted sounds

findings.mechanism: Programming directly addresses user needs and activities, making it a high priority for designers.
findings.quote: 3 out of 5 participants ranked the elements of importance as noted in the above list, with soundscape design and noise masking at the bottom.

findings.mechanism: Sustainability is a recognized important aspect of modern design, ranked highly by some experts.
findings.quote: The only variation was that interviewees C and P ranked sustainable design ahead of programming.

findings.mechanism: Visual aesthetics are traditionally central to landscape architecture and highly valued by experts.
findings.quote: they believed each of the first three factors listed above to be equally important.

findings.mechanism: Lack of familiarity with terminology and perceived lower importance leads to lower prioritization.
findings.quote: soundscape design and noise masking at the bottom.

findings.mechanism: Noise masking is often considered a reactive measure rather than an integrated design element, leading to lower prioritization.
findings.quote: soundscape design and noise masking at the bottom.

findings.antecedent: Noise mitigation strategies (berms, sound walls, wind direction consideration)
findings.mechanism: Physical barriers and environmental factors can reduce sound propagation.
findings.quote: prioritize “noise mitigation through berms, consideration of wind direction, and sound walls”

findings.antecedent: Intentional design elements (vegetation buffers, water features, program placement, natural elements)
findings.mechanism: These elements create a more pleasant and engaging sensory environment.
findings.quote: incorporating intentional vegetation buffers, water features, placement of programs, and natural elements into their designs to enhance human comfort.

findings.antecedent: Expected and appropriate sounds for context
findings.mechanism: Sounds that align with expectations reduce cognitive dissonance and enhance a sense of place.
findings.quote: People feel most comfortable in environments with expected and appropriate sounds for the context.

findings.antecedent: Unexpected sounds not aligned with surroundings
findings.mechanism: Disruption of expectations leads to negative perception and potential annoyance.
findings.quote: Unexpected sounds that do not align with the surroundings lead to a less pleasant environment.

findings.antecedent: Increase in positive 'people' sounds (laughter, talking, playing)
findings.mechanism: Human socialization sounds indicate activity and foster a lively, positive atmosphere.
findings.quote: An increase in positive “people” sounds... creates a more pleasant environment.

findings.antecedent: Good soundscape design principles (e.g., intimate gathering spaces away from streets, good buffers)
findings.mechanism: Thoughtful design creates harmonious auditory environments and places of refuge.
findings.quote: Implementing practical soundscape design principles significantly enhances public well-being

findings.mechanism: Past experiences, personal goals, emotional states, age, and abilities influence subjective interpretation.
findings.quote: Perception and preferences vary by person, context, and circumstances.

findings.antecedent: Visual stimuli (e.g., visual barriers, attractive plantings, color, uses, activation)
findings.consequent: Sense of security, enjoyment, and appreciation of appropriate sounds
findings.mechanism: Visual elements can block undesirable views, enhance aesthetics, and divert attention, improving overall experience.
findings.quote: Visual stimuli significantly impact the sense of security, enjoyment, and appreciation of sounds appropriate to the context.

findings.mechanism: Water creates white noise that audibly masks unwanted sounds.
findings.quote: Water is a widely used and effective method of masking noise

findings.mechanism: Vegetation provides a calming visual element that diverts attention from noise, reducing annoyance.
findings.quote: vegetation is a great visual distractor

findings.mechanism: Vegetation's physical properties do not significantly attenuate sound waves.
findings.quote: it is a common misconception that vegetation can significantly reduce or buffer traffic noise, although research has shown that it only minimally decreases noise levels.

findings.consequent: Spaces responsive to people of all abilities (relaxation, socialization, connection to nature)
findings.mechanism: Considering diverse sensitivities and needs ensures comfort and engagement for all users.
findings.quote: A healthy acoustic environment is essential for curating spaces that respond to people of all abilities.

findings.mechanism: Visual cues of traffic reinforce negative auditory perception, leading to psychological noise amplification.
findings.quote: the sound environment tends to be perceived as less pleasant when there is more visible traffic.

findings.antecedent: Visual presence of water or vegetation
findings.mechanism: Positive visual elements enhance the overall sensory experience and can psychologically mask unwanted sounds.
findings.quote: the visual presence of water or vegetation contributes to a more pleasant sound environment.

limitations: This study’s long-term trends and effectiveness must be fully addressed as this research solely captures the city at the time of the study.
Additional limiting factors include data collection timeframe, season/climate variables, and interviewee experience with soundscape design.

The ability to test and compare exact sound sources with different visual elements is limited since the onsite user surveys can only catch the current conditions, as many of the completed studies are tightly controlled in virtual environments.
The smaller sample size for certain locations may have influenced the data.
